passages.happening: God tells Ezekiel to set his face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them (verse 2). “O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD!” (verse 3). God will bring a sword against the mountains, hills, ravines and valleys, and destroy the high places. The altars will be torn down, the incense altars smashed, and the slain will lie before their idols (verses 3-6). ‘The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am the LORD’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
A high place was an outdoor shrine, often on a hill, with an altar and sometimes a standing stone, a wooden pole or a small building. Hills and green trees were thought to be places where the divine was near and fertility could be secured. Israelites often folded the worship of Baal and the fertility goddesses into their worship of the LORD.

Kings Hezekiah and Josiah had torn down these shrines and centered worship in Jerusalem, but Josiah died in 609 BC and his reforms did not last. By Ezekiel's day the local shrines were busy again.

Bodies left beside an altar defiled it completely, since contact with the dead made a person or place unclean. Josiah had used human bones to defile the shrines he destroyed.
passages.later: The law told Israel to destroy the places where the nations served their gods, ‘atop the high mountains, on the hills, and under every green tree’ (Deuteronomy 12:2). Josiah ‘covered the sites with human bones’ (2 Kings 23:14).
passages.asks: The mountains were where Israel felt closest to its other gods. Ask what places or habits draw your heart away from God. And ask what it would mean to give them up.

passages.happening:
‘Yet I will leave a remnant’ (verse 8). Scattered among the nations, the survivors will remember God, and how he was grieved by their unfaithful hearts and their eyes that lusted after idols. ‘So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done’ (verse 9), and they will know that God did not speak in vain (verse 10).

God tells Ezekiel to clap his hands, stamp his feet and cry out in lament for the house of Israel, who will fall by sword, famine and plague (verse 11). The slain will lie among their idols on every high hill and ‘under every green tree and leafy oak’ (verse 13), and the land will be laid waste ‘from the wilderness to Diblah’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Notice the word grieved in verse 9. God is not pictured as cold. He is wounded by his people's unfaithfulness, which Ezekiel will picture as adultery in chapters 16 and 23.

Clapping and stamping were gestures of strong feeling, here of lament. Under every green tree was a standard phrase for this kind of worship. No place called Diblah is known; many scholars think it is an early copying slip for Riblah, a town in Syria, so that the phrase covers the whole land from the southern wilderness to the north.
passages.later: Amos was told, ‘The end has come for My people Israel’ (Amos 8:2). Ezekiel later links the same loathing to God's forgiveness and new heart (Ezekiel 36:31).
passages.hard:
Why would God want survivors to loathe themselves? Isn't that harmful?

The phrase can sound like a call to self-hatred, and some readers have been hurt by teaching that pressed it that way. The Hebrew describes strong revulsion at one's own actions, the disgust a person feels on finally seeing clearly what they have done. In the chapter it goes with remembering God and knowing him (verses 9-10), and later Ezekiel links it to God's forgiveness and new heart (20:43; 36:31). It does not say that people are worthless. It says that sin, seen honestly, is ugly.

Christian tradition has distinguished this kind of sorrow, which leads to life, from a despairing shame that leads away from God, following Paul: ‘Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death’ (2 Corinthians 7:10). Shame that crushes is not what this passage asks for.
passages.asks: The survivors remembered how they had grieved God. Ask whether you see your sin as something that wounds him, not only something that breaks a rule. And ask what sorrow that leads to life would look like for you.
